Susan Maria Fowler Redmond

Master of Applied Science

Balloon-borne experiments present unique thermal design challenges. Radiation and conduction are

the predominant heat transfer mechanisms, with convection eﬀects being diﬃcult to characterize at an

altitude of 35–40 km. This greatly constrains the thermal design options and makes predicting ﬂight

thermal behaviour diﬃcult. SuperBIT aims to study weak gravitational lensing using a 0.5 m modiﬁed

Dall-Kirkham visible-to-near-UV telescope capable of achieving 0.02 ′′ stability [24]. To achieve the

theoretical resolution of 0.25 ′′ [23], mirror deformation gradients must be less than 15 nm and the

thermal environment must be stable on hour-long time scales. The 2018 test ﬂight served to collect data

for post-ﬂight characterization and to test the newly-developed heater control process. The post-ﬂight

characterization algorithm developed allows for parameter optimization, such as physical properties

or applied heat loads, based on the temperature proﬁle. An overview of the in-ﬂight heater control

performance, and extensive simulation results for the parameter-optimization-based thermal design are

presented here.

## Chapter 1

## Introduction

### 1.1 Motivation

On Earth, optical telescope capabilities and image quality are limited by atmospheric seeing. Moving

out into the far-UV or far-IR the atmosphere is mainly opaque reducing the science goals achievable

by ground-based telescopes. For these reasons, space telescopes were developed to improve data qual-

ity and probe wavelengths which are out of reach for ground-based instruments. Unfortunately, space

telescopes are very costly and have very long lead times [17]. Balloon-borne telescopes oﬀer a unique

compromise in which losses and costs are signiﬁcantly reduced. They ﬂy at altitudes ranging from 30 to

45 km in the stratosphere which provides a space-like environment but maintains gravity loading as seen

by ground-based instruments. Figure 1.1 shows the transmission gain for balloon instruments between

Near-Ultraviolet (NUV) and Near-Infrared (NIR) wavelengths when compared to ground-based instru-

ments either at sea level or the Hawaii Mauna Kea site. The current Super Pressure Balloon (SPB)

ﬂight duration record is 46 days [13] but that is expected to increase as developments continue. As

with satellites, mass and power consumption are major design optimization parameters which result in a

unique thermal design challenge due to the variability and uncertainty of the instrument loading. Histor-

ically the thermal design was determined through an iterative approach, and ﬂight results were not well

analyzed or documented. Improvements to both the characterization of the stratospheric environment,

and to the ability to predict the thermal performance of balloon-borne telescopes are desired.

SuperBIT is a 0.5 m diﬀraction-limited balloon-borne telescope which aims to study galaxy–galaxy

weak gravitational lensing. The science ﬂight is designed for a 100-day ﬂight on a Super-Pressure Balloon (SPB) out of Wanaka, NZ, in 2020. Weak lensing is an important cosmological probe capable

of constraining the matter density in the universe. As light from a source galaxy travels toward an

observer, foreground galaxies and dark matter act as lenses and distort the source galaxy image. Weak

lensing is a very powerful observational probe as it makes no assumptions on the ratio between dark

matter and baryonic matter. As implied by its name, the weak lensing signal is small, making it diﬃcult

to measure. This is compounded by the fact that any source of systematic error signiﬁcantly aﬀects

the measurement. Common instrument-induced issues are the size, shape, and stability of the point

spread function (PSF). Thermal variances in the instrument can aﬀect both the shape and stability

of the PSF. Gradients across the optical surfaces can cause aberrations and time-varying temperatures

induce correlated systematics that are diﬃcult to remove. For these reasons it is imperative that the

### 1.2 Stratospheric Thermal Environment

The stratosphere starts at an altitude of 10–18 km and transitions into the mesosphere at approximately

50 km [14]. The air pressure is low at 0.1 kPa and the temperature ranges from 222 to 278 K [14]. Note

that convection cannot be assumed to be zero until approximately 0.01 Pa. An interesting characteristic

of the stratosphere is that the ambient temperature increases with increasing altitude due to absorbed

UV radiation. Due to this temperature gradient, there is little convection between stratospheric layers.

There are, however, winds within the stratospheric layers which move the balloon throughout the ﬂight.

Temperature changes throughout day–night cycles also cause altitude variations due to pressure changes

in the balloon. This ampliﬁes the temperature drop at night as the balloon sinks to a cooler layer of

the stratosphere. To mediate this, it is possible to drop ballast making the payload lighter and thus

causing the balloon to rise, but this is only done in practice when signiﬁcant altitude changes occur.

Also, since balloon-borne telescopes operate close to the Earth and their trajectory is uncontrolled,

albedo and planetshine provide large, variable heat loads. The wavelength dependence of the incident

energy combined with the uncertainty in intensity hinders the loading prediction accuracy. Historically

the conduction and convective eﬀects of the residual atmosphere have been ignored but it is not clear

that this is a suitable assumption. For these reasons, the stratosphere is a challenging environment to

operate in, and diﬃcult to characterize.

### 1.3 Results of Previous Flights

The University of Toronto Balloon Astrophysics group currently has two balloon-borne telescope projects

underway. SuperBIT is a visible-to-near-UV telescope which studies the dark matter in galaxy clusters

and Spider is a microwave polarimeter which maps the cosmic microwave background (CMB). Both

telescopes have unique thermal design challenges; SuperBIT requires a high level of controllability,

while Spider requires mainly passive thermal control systems to reduce power consumption. Post-ﬂight

analysis of both instruments has revealed variations between the thermal model and the in-ﬂight data

that are not fully understood. As a result, the thermal systems in many cases are over-designed and yet under-perform. The desired solution to this problem would be to develop a ﬂexible, yet robust, design

method which can both update model parameters based on ﬂight data, and optimize model parameters

based on a desired temperature proﬁle. Such a method would yield more accurate prediction and control

of the thermal behaviour of both telescopes.

Previous SuperBIT ﬂights include a 2015 ﬂight with the Centre National d’´Etudes Spatiales (CNES)

and Canadian Space Agency (CSA) out of Timmins, ON, and ﬂights in 2016 and 2018 with NASA’s

Columbia Scientiﬁc Balloon Facility (CSBF). CSBF provides a Support Instrumentation Package (SIP)

which includes communication links as well as a number of sensors which provide a unique insight

to the stratospheric thermal environment [4]. These include multiple pyranometers, IR sensors, and

thermometers which measure the solar irradiance, planetshine, and free air temperature respectively.

Using these data as an input to the thermal model, it is possible to estimate the external heat loads on

the telescope more accurately.

### 1.4 Project and Signiﬁcance

This project is an inverse thermal control problem where the goal is to determine system thermal param-

eters given the desired outcome. These parameters can be either applied heat loads or a combination of

optical and thermophysical properties. A thermal design program capable of solving the inverse thermal

control problem would be very useful in the Balloon-borne Astronomy sector given the aforementioned

diﬃculty of characterizing balloon-borne instruments and their thermal environment.

The long term goal is to characterize thermal links, eﬀective emissivities, and component power

dissipation on the ground where the atmospheric contribution is relatively well known. These parameters

can then be used when analyzing test ﬂight data to predict the stratospheric contribution. Once this

is known, design modiﬁcations can be made to optimize the system based on the predicted conductive

and convective loading from the stratosphere. It would also allow for dynamic updating during ﬂight to

account for changes in the stratospheric load, optical properties, and heat loads. Since most telescopes

are used multiple times, ﬂight data based parameter updating facilitates quantiﬁed post ﬂight updates.

This thesis covers the development of the program to achieve this goal.

The development of this program will be primarily Matlab-based. However, it will also make use of

Thermal Desktop (TD), which has been used for past thermal analyses of both SuperBIT and Spider.

Thermal Desktop is quite powerful, and provides a convenient user interface for the development of

the physical model and mesh. TD alone does not provide the necessary customization for this project.

Therefore, a hybrid approach will be employed, in which TD will output a list of node numbers, and,

for each node, its associated subassembly, optical properties, view factors, and heat loads. This list

will then be fed into Matlab for the execution of the bulk of the analysis. The built-in calculation

of the view factors within TD, rather than in Matlab, provides a huge advantage, reducing both

complexity and computation time. This approach is justiﬁable, since the Monte Carlo ray tracer method

for the computation of view factors is a well-respected method in the ﬁeld of spacecraft thermal analysis.

### 2.1.1 Weak Lensing as a Cosmological Probe

Cosmology studies the large scale evolution of the universe. Λ Cold Dark Matter (ΛCDM) is the most

widely accepted model and assumes the universe contains radiation, matter, and dark energy. Each of

these components drive the temporal evolution of the universe as described by the Friedmann equation:

H2 = H2 0 � ΩRa−4 + ΩMa−3 + Ωka−2 + ΩΛ  , (2.1)

where the density parameters of each component, Ωi, relate the scale factor a of the universe – its size

– with its expansion rate H = ˙a/a and its current value H0 = 67.36 ± 0.54 km s−1Mpc−1 [21]. Since

there is currently no theoretical understanding of why these parameters have their speciﬁc values in our

Universe, the model parameters must be determined observationally; weak lensing provides a method of

constraining the matter density ΩM.

As previously mentioned, SuperBIT’s main science goal is to measure galaxy-galaxy weak gravita-

tional lensing for 100 clusters. This type of weak lensing uses galaxies at diﬀerent redshifts; a galaxy far,

far away as the source and a nearby galaxy cluster as the lens. The mass of the near galaxy cluster acts

as a gravitational lens and bends the light rays as shown by the white lines in Figure 2.1. Strong lensing

occurs when the lens galaxy is suﬃciently massive that it creates multiple images of the source galaxy

as shown by the red lines in Figure 2.1. Weak lensing is based on the same mechanism but produces

a milder distortion the image of the source galaxy shown in Figure 2.2 thats for illustrative purposes

only. The resulting image(s) depends on the not-necessarily-symmetric geometry of the whole system.

A perfectly symmetric system will create a single Einstein ring. Strong lensing is much more rare due

to the mass required to produce it, making weak lensing a more favourable observational probe.

### 2.1.2 Weak Lensing Measurement Error

Weak gravitational lensing is prone and sensitive to both statistical and systematic errors. One approach

for mitigating statistical errors is to restrict the scale at which the lensing signal is measured to the scale

at which the signal becomes comparable to the noise [27]. This is due to the issues that arise at either

extreme. At large scales there are fewer modes available to measure, and thus an increase in sample


<!-- Page 16 -->


Chapter 2. Background and Theoretical Basis 8

variance uncertainty. On the other hand, at small scales shape noise from the telescope beam begins

to dominate, decreasing the ability to measure the lensing signal. Another common issue is accurately

determining the redshift of the source galaxy. This is nominally done using photometric redshifts which

use crude ﬁlters and depend on strong features such as the Balmer break. This can be problematic as

the Lyman-α (Ly-α) feature can also be redshifted to the point that it appears to be the Balmer break, which is known as “photo-z degeneracy” [27]. A 1% change in the redshift of the source galaxy leads to

a 2% change in the power spectrum hence the source redshift must be known to the sub-percent level

[27]. The uncertainty in the source galaxy redshift can be reduced by using narrower ﬁlter bands over

a wider range such that both the Balmer and Ly-α features are visible or by comparing measurements

with large redshift surveys.

Instrument imperfections also contribute to errors in the weak lensing measurement. Misaligning or

over-constraining the optical surfaces can drastically aﬀect the point spread function (PSF). The PSF

describes the 2D intensity pattern that results when a point source is mapped to the image plane by the

telescope optics. If the PSF is not isotropic it can appear as a weak lensing signal as shown in Figure 2.5.

Imperfections in the optical surfaces as well as the wavelength-dependent nature of coatings cause the

PSF to change across the focal plane. Due to the ﬁnite number of stars in the sky, the PSF cannot be

characterized on every point on the focal plane thus interpolation is required. This interpolation can be

unconstrained so instrument models and heuristic methods are often used in parallel [27]. By dithering

the telescope between exposures, SuperBIT moves the image slightly on the focal plane, which further

facilitates characterization of the systematics.

*Figure 2.5: Eﬀect of PSF [10]*

In addition to changing across the focal plane, the PSF also changes with wavelength [27]. Repeating

observations in multiple bands using relatively narrow ﬁlters can aid in removing this systematic in the

post-processing. The last important PSF parameter is its overall size. As the PSF size increases with

respect to the galaxy size on the focal plane it dilutes the ellipticity measurement and increases the

required observing time [27].

When the images are corrected for the estimated systematics it is also possible to perform null tests

to check the correction success. One such test is to compute the correlation function between the PSF-

corrected galaxies and the star ellipticities in the original image [27]. Correlation between the two is a

good indicator that residual instrument systematics exist in the image.

### 2.2 The Parameter Updating Problem

When designing the thermal aspect of systems, the most common or traditional technique uses compo-

nent temperatures as the unknown parameters. Material properties as well as external heat loads are

used to calculate the temperature proﬁle of the system. If the proﬁle deviates from what is desired,

passive or active thermal control devices are implemented until the results are acceptable. Though this

has proven to be eﬀective it can be time consuming and requires an in depth understanding of heat

transfer and thermodynamics to be able to interpret the results and make eﬀective updates between

iterations. For these reasons, the inverse thermal design approach was introduced.

NASA uses two approaches within their Integrated Modeling of Optical Systems (IMOS) tool de-

veloped at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) [19]. Both concepts require the desired temperature

proﬁle as an input. One option is to input the thermophysical properties and solve for the required

additional heat loads, also known as the thermal control problem [19]. This is useful when the phys-

ical properties are well known, which is not always the case in the stratosphere or with sub-optimal

component contacts. The next option is to specify the heat loads and solve for the properties, or the

parameter updating problem [19]. This method is most applicable in radiation dominated environments

where optical properties can be customized with relative ease which is directly applicable to SuperBIT

and Spider. In both cases Papalexandris and Milman [19] prove that for a given temperature gradient

there is a unique set of parameters which are required. Ideally these two concepts will be combined for

this project to facilitate thermal control optimization.

There have also been methods developed to extrapolate experimental temperature proﬁle data to the

full thermal model [20]. Based on this approach, data from test ﬂights and thermal vacuum tests can

be used along with the previously discussed methods to update parameters creating a more accurate

model. Though they are still relatively new, they have been tested and found to be robust. In addition

to extrapolation techniques, understanding the thermal sensitivity of important components can aid

thermal design. Providing the model is accurate, it indicates the critical parameters that must be pre-

cisely implemented to maintain components within their respective allowable ranges. Many approaches

have been developed; the main one involves calculating the partial derivatives of the nodal equations

with respect to the design parameters [5]. Though the equations are nonlinear in temperature, they are

linear with respect to most design parameters including conductivity and external heat loads reducing

the complexity of the problem. It is also useful for parameter updating and thermal control problems

as providing the gradient of the objective function to the nonlinear solver can decrease the run time

and increase accuracy. It must be acknowledged that for SuperBIT the environment ﬂuctuates with the

day-night cycles and the irregular slew patterns when pointing at galaxy clusters. For this reason, the

sensitivities may change with time with some parameters being critical during the day and others during

the night.

### 2.5.2 Thermal Desktop Radiation Calculations

The radiation calculations are executed in TD by the RadCAD R ⃝function. TD calculates the radia-

tive energy exchanged between two nodes, deﬁned as “radks”[18], using the Monte Carlo method as a

“stochastic integration technique”[18]. Rays are isotropically and randomly shot from a given node and

traced around the model as they strike other surfaces. To maintain consistency between simulation runs,

the software allows the user to request that the same random sample is used at the start of each run.

The change in ray energy as it propagates is dependent on the optical properties deﬁned for the model

surfaces. It is important to note that if a surface face is set as ‘inactive’ the ray energy is altered as per

the emissivity of the inactive face but the change in energy is not applied to the node. If the emissivity

is set to unity the ray energy goes to zero when it strikes the inactive face; if it is set to zero the ray is

perfectly reﬂected. Setting the emissivity to zero is not recommended as it can lead to inﬁnite loops.

For active faces in the basic case, each ray’s energy is decremented by the absorptivity of each surface

it encounters until it reaches a user speciﬁed minimum (the ‘Energy CutoﬀFraction’) and is terminated.

The user speciﬁed minimum prevents the program from getting stuck in an inﬁnite loop but can also

produce inaccurate results if it is set too high. TD oﬀers an alternative which treats an absorptivity as

a probability that a ray will be completely absorbed. To implement this option the user must set the

‘Energy CutoﬀFraction’ value to one. When a ray encounters a surface it is either fully absorbed or

fully reﬂected with it’s energy unchanged. The ray tracing continues until all rays are absorbed. This

can be more CPU eﬃcient but tends to distribute the error non-uniformly with the error increasing with

distance from the emitting node. Note that this is only applied during radk calculation and not view

factor calculation. For both approaches it is obvious that the accuracy of the result is heavily dependant

on the number of rays shot by each node. If the average radk magnitude is known, the error for an

individual radk can be predicted using:

It is important to note that while TD oﬀers the functionality to calculate classic View Factors, they

are not used within the simulation unless speciﬁcally requested. When the traditional View Factor

approach is used it is assumed that a surface is uniformly loaded. By using the Monte Carlo approach

it allows the user to implement much coarser meshes as this method does not require uniform loading.

While the Monte Carlo method is powerful and eﬃcient, tracing all rays through an entire model

at once can be slow. To combat this, TD puts the model in a bounding box and divides it into eight

sub-boxes called ‘oct-cells’ as shown in Figure 2.8. It then continues to divide the oct-cells into more,

smaller oct-cells until the used speciﬁed maximum surfaces per cell is met. The result is that regions

with a denser mesh will also have more oct-cells. Once the model is suﬃciently subdivided the ray

tracing begins. The program only initially checks for collisions with surfaces within the same oct-cell as

### 3.3.1 Thermal control of SuperBIT Optics in the Stratosphere

Thermal control of optical surfaces is a well known challenge in astronomy. Static deformations on the

order of 15 nm and varying deformations over time can result in misleading weak gravitational lensing

measurements. It is thus desired to house the instrument in a static, isothermal environment and to have a well designed telescope which allows the optics to contract freely at ﬂoat. SuperBIT has a 1.9m

long temperature controlled baﬄe to maintain the optics at 273 K, rather than the ambient 233 K,

for the test ﬂights due to the thermal masses of the mirrors, sub-par mirror mounts, and steady state

temperature of the tertiary mirrors. The large thermal masses of the primary and secondary mirrors

require a setpoint temperature which allows them to stabilize post-launch in a reasonable amount of

time. It was predicted that the sub-optimal design of the engineering telescope would excessively deform

the mirrors if they were permitted to cool to the ambient 233 K. The science telescope will be installed

after the 2018 test ﬂight making this concern largely obsolete. Lastly, the optics box housing the tertiary

or tip-tilt mirror, shown in Figure 3.2, nominally reaches a temperature 273 K when the baﬄe heaters

are oﬀ. It is beneﬁcial to have all optics at the same temperature so 273 K was a logical setpoint.

The secondary mirror is enclosed in an aluminum housing reducing the eﬀectiveness of the temperature


<!-- Page 37 -->

controlled baﬄe. A heater is attached to a radiator plate located behind the secondary mirror which

provides additional control while avoiding gradients across the optical surface.

During the The 100 day SPB ﬂight from Wanaka, NZ, SuperBIT will experience extreme day and

night temperature conditions causing many of SuperBIT’s electrical and mechanical components to

require heaters. As of the 2018 test ﬂight there are a total of 30 heaters on the payload and each

heater is controlled using a standard proportional-integral-derivative (PID) control loop. To minimize

power and increase thermal stability, it is desired to have individual PID gains for each heater. As

previously discussed, the stratospheric environment is not well characterized so PID gains tuned on the

ground are not necessarily well suited to ﬂoat conditions. Also, for components with a large thermal

mass, tuning gains can take upwards of an hour. Manually tuning 30 heaters is thus time consuming

and impractical for a test ﬂight scenario where time is limited. For this reason an auto-tuning feature

has been implemented. Each heater-themistor-component system is modelled as an equivalent thermal

resistor-capacitor (RC) circuit, and a least-squares optimizer is used to ﬁnd the PID gains which minimize

overshoot and settling time. This is done using Matlab’s sequential quadratic programming function

fmincon described in Section 2.3. This function is relatively robust with respect to local minima and

invalid guesses.

### 4.1.1 Interface Overview

To implement this approach, the model is ﬁrst drawn in Thermal Desktop. The model can be validated

by running a simulation which includes ground atmospheric conditions and comparing the results to

data from ground operations. From here, various aspects of the thermal network can be exported taking

advantage of both TD’s aesthetic visual representation of the model and its eﬃciently implemented

Monte Carlo ray tracing technique for determining view factors between nodes. These ﬁles are then

imported into a Matlab code, where the main analysis is performed. A subset of the subassemblies

are chosen to have unknown parameters and the optimizer solves for the system that best represents

the user-deﬁned temperature proﬁle. The new temperature proﬁle and its error can then be plotted as

a colour-map in TD.

Thermal Desktop has many features that maximize the eﬃciency of the thermal design software. The

Matlab code was developed to read in the applicable TD output ﬁles in their respective formats. This

was a nontrivial task as many of the output ﬁles have variable header formats and a node numbering

technique had to be developed. In Thermal Desktop, the node numbering is local to each subassembly such that TELESCOPE.1 is diﬀerent than BALLOON.1. As such, the subassembly name must be

extracted and converted into a unique identiﬁer and then paired with the local node number. The

subassemblies are then sorted in ascending order and then paired with a simpler identiﬁer. This ensures

that the conversion is consistent for all portions of the code. All global node numbers have the same

number of digits where the ﬁrst three indicate the subassembly and the last four indicate the node

number within the subassembly; for example node 1000024 is the 24th node in subassembly 100. This

ensures the nodes stay with their subassembly when sorted. Also, surface nodes can have diﬀerent

optical properties on each side. To deal with this TD has an option to assign unique node numbers

to the top and bottom faces of surfaces. This will be a useful feature for future developments. In this

iteration of the code it was decided to keep it simple and surfaces either have the same optical properties

on both sides or they only have one side active. Since the outputs available from TD are somewhat

There are cases when the step size shrinks too quickly resulting in very small changes in the objective

sometimes better to provide an initial guess far from the predicted value to keep the steps larger for

longer. When this does occur it is fairly obvious with the output values being very similar to the initial

### 4.5.7 Results Summary

In testing this algorithm it was desired to cover a large portion of the parameter space. This was

accomplished by having two models with diﬀerent properties and heat loads and running extensive

simulations on both. For both models the optimization algorithm was able to solve for many emissivity

and conductivity combinations as well as the heat loads producing sub-kelvin temperature errors. It is

important to note that all simulations performed were for the steady-state case. As expected errors and

runtime tend to increase with the number of unknowns. As the system sensitivity on a parameter drops,

the error increases and the runtime either takes a sharp rise or a sharp dive. It will either run much

longer due to the fact that the steps are less eﬀective or it will hit the step tolerance very quickly and

exit even though the nodal temperature error is well above 1 K. Though the latter case is undesirable, a

warning is produced if the exit ﬂag is 2 (Table 2.3) and the large temperature error is a good indication

that the system did not properly converge as in Case 5a in Table 4.8. To mediate this the error weighting

can be increased or the initial guess can be altered. For conductivities with low system sensitivity it is

often best to have the initial guess very far from the predicted value to avoid the step size shrinking too

fast. SOI studies were performed on many sets of unknowns to demonstrate the optimizer’s capabilities.

In cases where the initial guess needs to be relatively close the two step approach shown in Table 4.7,

Case 5, has proved to be eﬀective.

Additional cases were also performed where the temperature distribution was not feasible for a

homogeneous material or alloted heat load locations. For example, the desired temperature for a node

with a heat load was increase by 10 K but the distribution around it was left the same. In these cases,

the result was sensitive to the weighting scheme. If the weighting was high on the altered node, it

converged well in that location but the temperature error around it was high. This is acceptable as

## Conclusions and Future Work

### 5.1 Conclusions

Balloon-borne telescopes operate in very harsh and variable thermal environments. Being able to predict,

characterize, and design for the stratosphere is extremely important. Major strides have been made to

do just that for the SuperBIT instrument. Measuring galaxy–galaxy weak lensing is very diﬃcult and

imposes very strict tolerances on the optical surfaces. A preliminary analysis has been performed on the

SuperBIT primary mirror showing eﬀorts to isolate it from external loading were not suﬃcient during

the 2018 test ﬂight. This is to be updated prior to the 2019 test ﬂight and is expected to drastically

improve with the new science telescope which has been designed with this in mind.

Thermal control is an important aspect of a successful SuperBIT ﬂight. The 2018 test ﬂight imple-

mented a new approach in which the PID gains were optimized on the ground prior to the ﬂight. This

was accomplished by modelling the thermistor-heater-component system as an RC circuit for which the

parameters could be determined using the temperature response to a step input of the heater. Using

this model, the PID gains could be optimized based on the desired steady state error, settling time, and

percent overshoot. Flight data shows that the gains did not perform as well at ﬂoat as they did on the

ground but there was still a signiﬁcant improvement over previous ﬂights. In many cases the steady

state error was reduced by an order of magnitude and the oscillation amplitude was reduced by a factor

of two. This was a very successful ﬁrst implementation of the process providing a very solid foundation to build on for the next ﬂight.

To aid in thermal design a parameter estimation code has been developed. This code uses outputs

from TD to create a Matlab thermal model which is then used to optimize various aspects of the model. The Matlab model compiled from the TD outputs is not perfect and there exists a temperature error

on the order of 1 K between the two. This is the result of discrepancies between the conductances and

view factors used in the TD simulation versus what is produced in the output ﬁles. If the Matlab–TD

error is large it is an indication that there are issues with either the TD simulation settings or the TD

model. An insuﬃcient ray request in the monte carlo algorithm can very quickly cause the two models

to diverge. Also, if edge contacts are deﬁned TD does not always fully incorporate them in the output

ﬁles. Once the Matlab model is created, either the thermophysical properties can be optimized or

the heat loads. As shown in Section 4.5, the optimization algorithm is quite robust to the number of

unknowns, combinations of unknowns, as well as the initial guess. SOI studies are provided for each
